title: Props.trade research round 1: six open points
method: 7 researchers + 7 independent adversarial verifiers; read-only onchain RPC, GMTrade source (v0.10.0 / HEAD 5841d106), vendor docs

result.point: Point 1: Can the Props.trade vault program own GMTrade orders and positions through a program-derived address (PDA) signing via CPI, with all proceeds going back to accounts the vault controls?
result.verdict: CONDITIONAL YES: a program address can own GMTrade positions. This is proven in the code and happens live on mainnet, so the design is not broken. It does need one empty program address per trader, a bot that tells the vault about fills (callbacks are not available), and handling of payouts that are not USDC.

findings.claim: The receiver (where decrease output and profit go) can differ from the owner. Only the owner sets it, at creation. It is stored in the order and no later instruction can change it. findings.claim:
What happens when an order fails, expires or is cancelled:
- A failed execution (soft fail) marks the order Cancelled. For increases, the USDC goes back into the order's escrow and is then returned to the owner's token account when the order closes.
- Market orders expire after the store's configured request window.
- The owner can cancel a pending order at any time.
- The keeper can close an order only after it has completed or been cancelled.
- If the receiver's token account does not exist, the keeper's close is skipped and the funds wait in escrow until the owner closes the order.

findings.claim: Callbacks are NOT available to Props.trade. On mainnet, the program GMTrade calls after execution must be on a hard-coded allowlist, and the only entry is GMTrade's competition program. Your vault program therefore cannot be notified of fills. corrections_to_chat: The 'make-or-break' risk is resolved in Props.trade's favour. GMTrade does not require a normal wallet as owner. Both GMTrade's own treasury program and at least one outside program already own and trade GMTrade positions through program addresses on mainnet.

The chat assumed one vault address owns the positions. It must be one separate, empty program address per funded trader. A shared owner would merge different traders' positions in the same market into one position, and the account holding the vault's own data cannot be the owner.

The receiver can be set separately, but refunded collateral, liquidation proceeds and rebates always go to the owner. So in practice owner = receiver = the per-trader program address, and the vault then sweeps from there.
'USDC only' is not guaranteed on payout. Profits on longs can arrive as the market's long token (e.g. wrapped SOL) if the automatic swap to USDC fails or is not requested.

The drawdown auto-close does not have to rely only on the offchain bot for each position. The vault can place native GMTrade stop-loss orders, which GMTrade's keepers execute. An account-wide limit across several positions still needs your own bot.
result.recommended_action_or_wording:
Proceed with the PDA design. Minimal flow for the vault program (all GMTrade calls are CPIs signed with the per-trader PDA's seeds; the trader never signs for GMTrade):

SETUP, once per funded account:
1. Derive owner = PDA["funded", vault, account_id]. It must hold no data; keep the vault's state in a separate PDA. Fund it with about 0.05 SOL.
2. CPI prepare_user (the owner signs and pays).
3. Create the owner's ATAs for USDC and for each allowed market's long and short token.

OPEN (MarketIncrease):
4. Move the allocated USDC from the vault into the owner's USDC ATA.
5. Create the order escrow ATAs (authority = order PDA ["order", store, owner, nonce]) for the collateral, long and short tokens.
6. CPI prepare_position.
7. CPI create_order_v2 with:
   - owner = receiver = PDA;
   - source = the PDA's USDC ATA;
   - no callback accounts;
   - should_unwrap_native_token = false;
   - acceptable_price set;
   - the program enforcing allowed markets, max size and max leverage.
8. Optionally CPI create_order_v2 with StopLossDecrease or LimitDecrease for native stop-loss and take-profit orders.

CLOSE:
- Create the escrows, then CPI create_order_v2 MarketDecrease with decrease_position_swap_type = PnlTokenToCollateralToken and final output = USDC.

CANCEL:
- CPI close_order_v2 with executor = owner = receiver = rent_receiver = PDA.

SYNC (a permissionless crank):
- Read GMTrade's Position account (check that it is owned by Gmso1u… and matches the PDA seeds) and the PDA's token balances.
- Update the trader's equity and drawdown.
- Close any completed orders the keeper left open.
- Swap any non-USDC payouts.
- Sweep funds back to the vault.

Never let traders pass their own receiver, source account, referrer or builder-fee accounts.

Suggested hackathon wording: "Each funded account is a program-owned GMTrade account: our Solana program opens and closes GMTrade positions for the trader, and the trader can never withdraw the capital."
unresolved: GMTrade's keepers are run offchain by GMTrade and are not in this repo. The code has no rule against program-owned orders, and they are observed filling them. Nothing, however, stops GMTrade from filtering such orders later, and the store program is upgradeable (authority 6qp7ve…). The callback allowlist itself was added after an audit.
The mainnet request-expiration window and other store amounts (for example MinPositionAgeForManualClose) were not decoded, so I don't know how long a market order waits before it expires.

The amount of compute and the number of accounts one vault instruction can use when it bundles ATA creation, prepare_position and create_order_v2 were not measured. Flipper splits this into two instructions (PrepareGmtradeLeg + ExecuteTradeWithCollateral), and GMTrade's SDK uses address lookup tables. You will likely need both.
2 of the 8 sampled 'completed but unclosed' orders had receiver token accounts that existed, so the missing-token-account explanation does not cover every stuck order.
Flipper's (FQ8Uuy…) source code is not published or verified, so its design was inferred from transaction logs only.
GMTrade's user terms were read through a tool summary, not verbatim. Legal fit of a prop-firm model with pooled capital (and the ban on US persons) was not assessed.

result.point: Point 1: can the Props vault program own GMTrade positions? Is there precedent, and what does a real integration look like?
result.plain_answer: Yes. A program-controlled account can own GMTrade orders and positions, and this is already happening on mainnet. GMTrade's own treasury program does it in the public code. Two outside trading apps, Imperial and Flipper, run programs that open GMTrade positions in accounts only their program controls. I found 797 such program-controlled trader accounts on mainnet. So this is not the make-or-break risk the chat called it. What remains is ordinary engineering: give each funded trader their own program-controlled account, keep a little SOL in it for fees, and set up its token accounts ahead of time. Closing a position still takes two steps: the vault program asks for the close, and GMTrade's own bots carry it out a few seconds later. Devnet testing is possible, with limits: GMTrade's devnet runs, but its test USDC cannot be minted. The "builder fee" feature, which would let an app earn a cut of each trade, is not live yet.
result.verdict: CONFIRMED: a vault program can own GMTrade positions. GMTrade does it in its own code, and two live apps (Imperial, Flipper) do it on mainnet today. The chat's "make-or-break unknown" is settled.

corrections_to_chat: 'Make-or-break: can a PDA own a GMTrade position?' is already answered: yes. GMTrade's own treasury program does it (programs/treasury/src/instructions/swap.rs:146-193), and two live third-party programs (Imperial, Flipper) do it on mainnet for hundreds of users. It is no longer an open risk.

The stop-loss cannot be 'automatic' in the sense of Props closing the position itself. Props' program can only request a decrease order; GMTrade's permissioned keepers execute it, typically within seconds. The vault also cannot get onchain fill notifications: the callback hook is allowlisted to GMTrade's competition program only, so an offchain keeper or indexer is required.

'Use GMTrade through their open-source gmsol SDK' is only half right. The onchain vault calls GMTrade through the gmsol-programs crate (IDL plus declare_program!, anchor-lang 0.31.1) or gmsol-store with its `cpi` feature. The npm and Rust SDKs are offchain client libraries.

'Test on devnet first' is possible but harder than implied. GMTrade's devnet USDC mint has no mint authority, so you cannot mint test USDC. Devnet activity is sparse (last position trade 2026-08-28), and the devnet binary differs from mainnet's.

One vault PDA for all traders would merge their positions. GMTrade position addresses are derived from the owner, so each funded account needs its own signer PDA, funded with a little SOL, with its token accounts created in advance.

Builder fees are not a revenue option right now: unreleased, not deployed on mainnet or devnet, cap defaults to 0. For a vault that owns the capital they would mostly pay the vault's own money to itself. Today GMTrade's only built-in integrator reward is referral GT.
result.recommended_action_or_wording: Build it the way GMTrade's own treasury program does (programs/treasury/src/instructions/swap.rs). For each funded account, the Anchor vault derives a data-less signer PDA, e.g. seeds ["funded", trader, account_id]. The vault funds that PDA with a small SOL buffer and creates its USDC token account. It then calls prepare_user, prepare_position and create_order_v2 on GMTrade, signed by that PDA, with owner = receiver = the PDA. It checks the trader's risk limits before each call. Depend on gmsol-programs = "0.10" with anchor-lang 0.31.1. A trader-signed "close" instruction and a keeper-signed "force close" instruction both create a MarketDecrease order. Track order state (pending, cancelled, filled) offchain from the order and position accounts. Optionally set a GMTrade referrer through the same kind of call for the 10% fee discount. Suggested plain wording for the pitch: "Your funded account is a GMTrade position owned by the Props vault program. You can trade it, but only the program can move the money. Our risk bot watches your drawdown and, if you hit the limit, tells the program to close your trade; GMTrade fills the close within seconds." Avoid "the smart contract closes it automatically". For devnet, ask GMTrade for test USDC or use WSOL-collateral markets; otherwise test on mainnet with a few dollars.

result.corrected_plain_answer:
Yes. Your vault program can own GMTrade trades, so the design is not broken. I re-read GMTrade's code and checked live mainnet data myself. GMTrade only checks that the owner approved an action. It never checks whether the owner is a person's wallet or a program. GMTrade's own treasury already works this way, and so do at least two outside trading apps: their live trades were opened by their programs and paid out to accounts only those programs control. 797 of GMTrade's 33,616 user accounts belong to programs. Outside the owner, the only party that can act on these accounts is GMTrade's own bots. They can fill trades, liquidate losing ones, and send money back to your account. They cannot send it anywhere else. So the trader cannot withdraw, as long as your program decides where money goes.

What you must build around it:
- One separate, empty program-controlled account per funded trader, topped up with a little SOL. One shared account would merge different traders' trades into one.
- Your program must fix where money goes, which markets are allowed, and the size and leverage. Never pass the trader's choices straight through.
- Trades fill in two steps, a few seconds apart. GMTrade will not notify your program, so a small bot has to sync results. Market orders that don't fill expire after 30 minutes.
- Profits can come back as wrapped SOL or plain SOL, not only USDC, so your sweep has to convert them.
- New and important: stock, forex, gold and oil markets close outside trading hours. While they are closed, neither your bot nor a stop-loss can close a trade, so a weekend price jump can lose more than the 5% limit. The only hard ceiling is the money put into that trade. The safest fix is to put in as collateral only what the trader is still allowed to lose.
- A trader could still game you by losing on purpose into a pool they own a share of, or by betting both ways across two funded accounts. Your own rules need to cover that.
- GMTrade's team can upgrade its program, so these rules could change later.

The missing-token-account trap is real for program owners today. All 30 unclosed completed orders owned by programs on mainnet are MarketDecrease orders, and in every one of the 8 I sampled the escrow held dust (often a few lamports of wSOL) in a token the program address had no account for. That locks roughly 0.02+ SOL of rent per order until the owner closes it. Either create the program address's token accounts for USDC and every market's long and short token in advance, or set should_unwrap_native_token = true so wSOL arrives as plain SOL. Also build a 'close finished order' step, as Flipper (close_gmtrade_settlement_order) and Imperial (close_filled_native_order) did.

Native stop-loss and take-profit orders stay open after a position is closed (GMTrade docs). Positions are keyed by owner, market, collateral and side, so a leftover stop-loss would fire against the trader's next position in that market. Native stop-losses are not a hard loss cap. result.corrected_plain_answer:
Yes. Your vault program can hold and trade GMTrade positions itself, so the design is not broken.

GMTrade only checks that the owner approved each request. It does not care whether that owner is a person's wallet or a program. Evidence that this works:
- GMTrade's own treasury program does it (for swaps).
- A live app, Flipper, did it on mainnet as recently as 22 September 2026.
- Another app, Imperial, did it from April to June 2026.
- About 800 GMTrade accounts are held by programs rather than people.

What you need to plan for:
- **One account per trader.** Give each funded trader their own program-held account with a little SOL in it (about 0.05). One shared account would merge different traders' trades in the same market.
- **Every open or close is two steps.** Your program places the request, then GMTrade's own bots carry it out, usually about 4 seconds later. A market request that is not filled within 30 minutes is dropped.
- **GMTrade will not tell your program when a trade fills.** Its "notify me" feature only works for GMTrade's own competition program, on both mainnet and devnet. You need your own bot, or a follow-up step that reads the result. Flipper built exactly this ("confirm fill" and "timeout" steps).
- **Set up token wallets first.** Before trading, create the account's token wallets for USDC and for each market's other token. If one is missing, even a tiny leftover amount leaves the order unfinished and its deposit stuck until your program closes it. 30 such stuck orders held by programs exist on mainnet today.
- **Payouts are not always USDC.** Profits can arrive in another token, for example wrapped SOL.
- **Built-in stop-loss orders help, but are not a guarantee.** GMTrade has stop-loss and take-profit orders run by its bots, and your program could place them. But:
  - they fill at the market price and can stall in fast moves;
  - they stay open after a position closes, so they would hit the trader's next trade in that market unless your program cancels them;
  - no program-held stop-loss is live on mainnet today to copy.

  A 5% limit across a whole account still needs your own bot.
- **GMTrade can change its rules.** It can upgrade its program with 4 of 7 signers and a 10-minute delay. An unreleased update already adds a new rule for opening trades.
- **Devnet testing is limited.** A GMTrade test network exists with 34 markets, but its test USDC cannot be minted, and I did not see its bots fill any trades recently.

Tools: the onchain vault should use GMTrade's Rust package gmsol-programs 0.10.0 (with Anchor 0.31.1). The npm SDK 0.10.0 is for your website and bot, not the vault.

result.point: Point 3: what is honestly onchain, and can the stop-loss move onchain?
result.plain_answer: Don't call Props.trade "decentralised". What you can honestly say is that funded accounts are onchain: real GMTrade positions, paid for by a Solana vault, with public trades and payouts. The loss cap can move onchain today without any bot you run. The vault puts up only the amount a trader is allowed to lose, and GMTrade's own liquidation closes the trade when that money is gone. A GMTrade stop-loss order is a useful extra, but GMTrade says it isn't guaranteed. It can be cancelled without warning, and it can't fire while a stock or gold market is shut. Anyone can be allowed to trigger a close through your program, but GMTrade's own 8 approved bots still have to carry it out. The challenge stays on your servers. The most you can do is make it hard to tamper with and easy to check, so say that plainly.
result.verdict: CORRECTED. "Decentralised prop firm" goes too far. "Onchain funded accounts" is true and still strong, and a hard loss cap enforced by GMTrade's liquidation works today with no Props server involved.

corrections_to_chat: "Decentralised prop firm" goes too far. The challenge runs on Props servers, and Props will hold upgrade and pause keys. GMTrade itself is controlled by a 4-of-7 multisig (10-minute delay) that can upgrade it and switch off trading features. Only 8 approved GMTrade bots can carry out any order or liquidation.

"The smart contract handles risk limits" is false as written. The challenge limits are offchain. For funded accounts, the contract enforces the limit only if you build it (a loss budget posted as collateral, or a close instruction anyone can trigger). GMTrade orders can't express a total loss across several positions.

"The position gets closed automatically" needs a condition. A GMTrade stop-loss is carried out by GMTrade's bots, and GMTrade says it isn't guaranteed. If it fails it is cancelled, not frozen (the GMTrade docs say frozen, but the Solana code has no such state). It can't run while a stock, gold or forex market is closed. Liquidation is the only close that always applies.
The chat assumed a Props-run bot was the only way. Posting only the loss budget as collateral lets GMTrade's liquidation enforce the hard cap with no Props server.

"Priced off the same feed as the venue" is harder than assumed. GMTrade prices come from Chainlink Data Streams (all 3,783 feed accounts), which needs Chainlink's approval. Pyth's price service has needed an API key since 2026-08-26.

Propr, the name-risk competitor, is not a real-money onchain prop firm. Its own disclosure says all accounts, funded ones included, are 100% simulated. Props.trade's real funded positions are a genuine difference you can point to.

(a) Post only the loss budget as collateral. GMTrade's liquidation then enforces the hard cap.
(b) Place a GMTrade stop-loss with no price limit, sized to close the whole position, as a softer early exit. Re-place it if it gets cancelled.
(c) Add a close instruction anyone can trigger for the daily limit, with a safety margin for the Pyth feed's lag. Its close orders still need GMTrade's bots.
(d) Store each account's rules when it opens. Allow pause to stop new trades only, never closes or payouts. Put upgrade and admin keys in a Squads multisig with a delay.
(e) Hash the challenge trades onchain and publish the list of trades.
Avoid these words: decentralised, guaranteed, yield, investment, "we pay you".

result.corrected_plain_answer:
Don't call Props.trade a "decentralised prop firm". The challenge runs on your servers. GMTrade itself is run by a 4-of-7 multisig with a 10-minute delay, and only 8 addresses approved by GMTrade can carry out any trade or liquidation.

What you can honestly say: funded accounts are real GMTrade positions, paid for by a Solana vault, and every funded trade and payout is public.

The strongest honest safety claim is structural. If the vault only ever puts up the amount a trader is allowed to lose, it can never lose more than that on a trade. GMTrade positions can't go into debt, so this holds even if a close is late. GMTrade's liquidation then closes the trade. But that is done by GMTrade's approved bots, not guaranteed on timing, and GMTrade can switch it off. None of this has been built or tested yet, so say "designed to", not "works today".

A GMTrade stop-loss is only an extra. GMTrade says it isn't guaranteed. It can be cancelled without warning, including when the price has already jumped past the point where the collateral covers the loss. It can't fire while a stock or gold market is shut, and the real risk there is the price jump when the market reopens.

To keep the "trader can't take the money" promise, your program must send every trade's proceeds back to the vault. Any "we can't change the rules" line is only true once your upgrade key is locked or behind a delay.

The challenge stays offchain. The most you can do is make it tamper-evident and publish the trade list.

Against Propr, real funded positions are a real difference: Propr's own terms say every account is 100% simulated. Carrot does copy some trades with real money, though, and Hyro is building a similar Solana vault, so don't claim you're the only one.

For the copy, change "GMTrade closes the position itself" to "GMTrade's liquidation system closes it". Change "a bit past the limit" to "past the limit". Change "Your funded account doesn't [run on our servers]" to "Your funded account is onchain, and we can't withdraw from it", and only say the second part if it's true.

result.point: Point 4: the real tech stack for building Props.trade on GMTrade (replacing the guessed hackathon Q3 answer)
result.plain_answer: The guessed stack was mostly right, with three real mistakes. First, GMTrade prices every trade with Chainlink Data Streams only. It does not use Pyth, so "Pyth" should come out, and the practice challenge has to use Chainlink prices too. Those prices are not free: Chainlink charges from $150 a month per price feed, with no free tier. The only no-cost way to get the same numbers is GMTrade's own price service, which their website uses but which is not documented for outside use. Second, the GMTrade toolkit is written in Rust. The TypeScript version is a Rust build packaged for JavaScript, and the newest copy on npm is empty; the last working one is 0.9.0 from February. The vault program also has to stay on Anchor 0.31, not the current Anchor 1.x. Third, the code is not "open source". It is under a Business Source License, which allows non-production use until December 2027. The stop bot needs a server that is always on, not Vercel. Vercel, Supabase and Privy are free choices, not requirements. Privy does support Solana embedded wallets today.
result.verdict: CORRECTED: remove Pyth and add Chainlink Data Streams; pin Anchor 0.31 and the gmsol 0.10.0 packages; the JavaScript toolkit is a Rust build with a broken latest release; the code is source-available (BUSL), not open source; the stop bot needs an always-on server.

Corrected Q3 answer (paste-ready): "Solana, USDC, an Anchor 0.31 Rust vault program that trades on GMTrade (GMX v2 on Solana) through their gmsol-programs crate, GMTrade GM pools as counterparty, Chainlink Data Streams prices (the same oracle GMTrade settles on), a TypeScript risk bot on an always-on server using GMTrade's JS/WASM SDK, Next.js on Vercel, Supabase, Privy embedded Solana wallets. AI tools: [ai] and AI tools."

Per item:
- Solana: REQUIRED. GMTrade only runs there.
- USDC: REQUIRED (by our design). GMTrade uses the standard Circle USDC mint (EPjF...Dt1v), so the vault can hold the same token.
- Anchor 0.31 Rust vault program: REQUIRED. Only an onchain program can own positions and hold funds. It must be Anchor 0.31.x to link with gmsol-programs 0.10.0 (^0.31.1); GMTrade itself builds with Anchor 0.31.1 and Solana 2.1.21.
- gmsol-programs crate (Rust, v0.10.0): REQUIRED for the vault to call GMTrade. Pin 0.10.0 to match mainnet, not repo HEAD.
- GMTrade GM pools as counterparty: REQUIRED. That is where winners are paid from.
- Chainlink Data Streams: REQUIRED as the price source (GMTrade accepts nothing else on mainnet). How the sim gets those prices is a CHOICE: (a) a paid Data Streams subscription, from $150/month per feed, self-serve at app.chain.link; (b) GMTrade's free but undocumented keeper price API (ask GMTrade before relying on it); onchain price accounts are too stale to act as a live price ticker.
- TypeScript risk bot on an always-on server: REQUIRED that some always-on offchain watcher exists (no onchain fill notifications for outside programs; account drawdown spans positions). The language is a CHOICE: TypeScript works with @gmsol-labs/gmsol-sdk 0.9.0 (loads in Node 22) plus the vault's Anchor TS client; Rust gets the fuller official client. Per-position stop-loss orders can also be left to GMTrade's own keepers.
- Next.js on Vercel: CHOICE. Fine for the website, but not for the bot.
- Supabase: CHOICE. Any database works; the sim state just needs to live somewhere.
- Privy embedded Solana wallets: CHOICE. Verified supported (react-auth 3.45.0). The alternative is the standard Solana wallet adapter (what GMTrade itself uses).
- Paid Solana RPC: effectively REQUIRED for a real bot (public RPC is rate-limited). Provider is a CHOICE.
- [ai] / AI tools: CHOICE (your tooling).
Also drop the words "open-source" for GMTrade; say "source-available".

result.corrected_plain_answer:
The guessed stack was mostly right. Five things need fixing, and one more point needs a caveat.

1. Prices. Today GMTrade prices every trade on mainnet with Chainlink Data Streams. I checked all 78 tokens onchain, and there are 3,783 price accounts, every one of them Chainlink. So drop "Pyth" from the Props.trade stack and say Chainlink. The caveat: GMTrade's own docs call Pyth and Switchboard backups, and GMTrade's operators can switch any of 34 tokens to Pyth whenever they want. The practice challenge should check which price source each token uses rather than assume Chainlink forever.

2. Getting those prices is not free the official way. Chainlink sells them from $150 a month per feed, with no free tier. Pyth's public service now needs a key too (since August 26, 2026). GMTrade runs its own price service, which its website uses. It answered my test with no key, but it is undocumented and has no published rules, so ask GMTrade before building on it.

3. The GMTrade toolkit is written in Rust. The JavaScript version is the same Rust code compiled to run in JavaScript, and GMTrade's own website uses it. The newest copy on npm is empty, though. The last working copy (0.9.0, February) is older than some fixes to the profit-and-loss math. The safer path is to build the JavaScript package yourself from the 0.10.0 release, which is what mainnet runs (deployed August 12, 2026).

4. The vault program has to stay on Anchor 0.31. Neither Anchor 0.32 nor the current 1.x will work with GMTrade's code library.

5. GMTrade's code is not "open source". It is under a Business Source License, which allows non-production use until December 2027 at the latest. GMTrade's own terms loosely call it open source, but the correct term is "source-available". Ask GMTrade before a real-money launch.

The stop bot needs a server that is always on. Vercel can only wake a job once a minute at best, which is too slow for a stop-out on leveraged positions. The drawdown rule itself can live inside the vault program so anyone can check it, but something offchain still has to trigger it.

Next.js on Vercel, Supabase and Privy are free choices, not requirements. Privy does support Solana embedded wallets today. GMTrade's own app uses the standard Solana wallet connector.

GMTrade also runs on devnet, the free test network, with the same addresses. That could be used for the demo. I did not confirm that orders actually get filled there.

result.corrected_plain_answer:
Checked again at 02:35–02:43 IST on 23 Sept (21:05–21:13 UTC on 22 Sept) against DefiLlama, GMTrade's own data feed and the blockchain directly.

The pool sizes are right. GMTrade holds about $28.2M in total (down about 11% in a month, not exactly 10.8%). The money that actually pays winning traders is about $1.17M in the SOL pool, $0.83M in BTC, $0.87M in ETH and $1.80M in gold. My own blockchain read gave exactly these figures.

The main correction to the researcher: the 21 Sept '$1.2–2.4M per pool' was probably not the inflated 'spare trading room' number. It matches the real deposit figures DefiLlama showed for SOL and gold on 18–21 Sept. The '$25–50K max position' came from applying gold's pool, the biggest, to every major market, and pools have shrunk since (gold down 22% since 19 Sept, BTC down 19% since 20 Sept). The 'spare room' number ($2.2–3.6M per pool, $90M in total) is still not deposited money and should not be quoted.

Using the chat's own rule (one position no bigger than 1–2% of the pool), the biggest sensible position today is about $12–23K on SOL, $8–17K on BTC, $9–17K on ETH and $18–36K on gold. That makes the old $25–50K 2–3 times too high for SOL, BTC and ETH, but only about 1.4 times too high for gold. If you apply the rule to the half of the pool that pays a given side, halve those numbers.

Starting with $5K accounts, or $10K accounts with little or no leverage, in the SOL, BTC, ETH and gold pools is still a sensible, careful launch size. Three things to add:
1. Pool sizes can change within a day. Most of the BTC, ETH and gold pool money sits in GMTrade's automatic vaults, which can move it between markets, so check pool sizes daily.
2. Gold is the most crowded pool, not the safest one. Bets on gold are about 8 times the gold pool's money, and there is only about $0.3M of room left for new bets that gold will fall.
3. The 200–260% yields shown for these pools count only fees and come from GMTrade itself. SOL and BTC pool investors actually lost a little money over the last week.

Trading volume: the 30-day totals are right ($24.0B traded, $3.34M in fees). The 'volume fell 75–85% since 19 Sept' claim is overstated, because two of those days were a weekend, when volume is always low. Weekday volume is still clearly down (Monday was 58–83% below earlier Mondays), and the number of daily traders fell sharply even compared with earlier weekends. Points farming is confirmed by Galaxy Research, and GT points were still being minted at 02:41 IST on 23 Sept.
